OCP GLOBAL SUMMIT 2026, DAY 2 ANALYSIS SO FAR (1/6)
Tuesday, October 13, 2026, start of day through about 12:00 PM PT
Companion to the Day 1 complete analysis and to the Day 1 transcript deep dive

SCOPE AND COVERAGE NOTE

This report covers Day 2 of the OCP Global Summit 2026, Tuesday, October 13, 2026, from the start of the day through about 12:00 PM PT. It is built the same way as last night's Day 1 report: coverage on X first, item by item, with every claim carrying its sourcing and its confidence level, and web research second, used to find the primary sources behind the posts and the announcements that never appeared on X. Nothing from Day 1 is re-reported as Day 2 news. Day 1 material appears only where a Day 2 development resolves, updates, or contradicts a Day 1 item, and those cross references are labeled as Day 1 carryover wherever they appear.

Three source streams were used. First, coverage on X through the morning: 2,858 posts across the event record, with today producing 5 headline items and 2 roundups (06:21 PT and 09:34 PT, the second covering 43 posts). A further 23 items posted this morning had not been headlined by midday; they are reported here from the X record. Second, the Day 1 transcript deep dive published this morning, which pulled the auto captions of all 50 Day 1 session videos posted to the OCP YouTube channel (143,546 words of transcript). Those transcripts are Day 1 evidence, recorded Monday, October 12. They matter to a Day 2 report for one reason: Section 10 of last night's report assigned 15 questions to today, and the transcripts, which arrived after last night's report was written, already settle or advance several of them. Where a status below rests on the transcripts, it says so, and the genuinely new October 13 development is stated separately. Third, web research run today on October 13 publications: vendor press releases (Business Wire, PR Newswire, GlobeNewswire), the OCP Foundation, and trade coverage, each cited with its source and date in the sources section.

What remains today after midday: the DMTF Manageability Workshop runs 1:00 PM to 5:00 PM PT; the Arista talk by Andy Bechtolsheim, The Gigawatt AI Data Center Era, runs 1:00 PM to 1:25 PM PT and was imminent at midday; Meta's IceCube session on Broadcom TH6C is at 1:25 PM PT; a Marvell Expo Hall Theater talk is at 1:50 PM PT; the IPEC near package optics workshop is at 2:00 PM PT and is listed as not recorded; Samsung's CXL pools and SSD KV cache session is at 2:50 PM PT; NVIDIA's 800 VDC session is at 4:05 PM PT; and NVIDIA's Spectrum-X optics session is at 4:30 PM PT and is listed as not recorded. The AI memory wall panel is Wednesday, October 14, 5:30 PM to 8:30 PM PT, not today. Section 11 lists the full watch list.

One timing warning that shapes the whole report, because it is the single largest error risk in this material: most of the big keynote linked launches that search returns for "today" are dated October 12, Day 1. Microsoft's Maia 300 launch is dated October 12. AMD's Helion release is dated October 12. The KIOXIA CM9 direct liquid cooling release is dated October 12. The Celestica DS6005 release is dated October 12. The Texas Instruments 3 chip launch is dated October 12. Those items appear in this report only where today produced something new about them (a primary source located, a corroborating cluster reported, a Section 10 question answered), and each one is dated plainly where it appears. The genuinely October 13 primary releases found are: Marvell's Alaska retimer and AEC DSP launch, Credo's OmniConnect Weaver release, the OCP and IDC Market Impact Study, the Wiwynn, Ayar Labs and GUC live CPO demonstration release, the Semtech and Tower SiGe capacity release, the nVent and AMD Helios cooling release, Astera Labs' Aries 7 PCIe 7 portfolio, the Lattice and AMI SCMP workstream launch, SolarEdge's 800 VDC showcase release, and Wistron's summit showcase release.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Day 2 so far is a day of confirmations and specifications rather than new platform launches. The overnight and morning coverage produced 5 headline items. Marvell launched the Alaska E 3.2T protocol aware retimer and the second generation Alaska A 1.6T AEC DSP (MarvellTech; the post is a launch graphic with the 224G per lane and 102.4T context in its text and no product specifications, which come from Marvell's October 13 Business Wire release). Marvell also demonstrated what it calls the industry's first 2nm 400G per lane PAM4 solution live at Booth B31 (MarvellTech, photo of the booth screen with live Keysight eye diagrams: RLM 0.944, TDECQ 0.50 dB, Outer ER 3.976 dB, Outer OMA 775.0 uW, Average Power -0.33 dBm, frame trigger 226.67000 GBd). Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and Global Unichip (GUC) ran the first live co-packaged optics demonstration of the summit, a Wiwynn compute system with a GUC ASIC package carrying Ayar TeraPHY optical engines lit by a SuperNova external light source, streaming real time health telemetry (carrioresearch, corroborated by the companies' October 13 PR Newswire release). The OCP Foundation announced the 2026 IDC Market Impact Study, which raises the 2029 forecast for OCP recognized IT equipment spending by 2.7x to $800B and projects $892B in 2030, 51% of the covered categories, with $628B of it AI related (OpenComputePrj, infographic viewed and verified against the Foundation's own release). Credo's OmniConnect Weaver memory fanout was demonstrated on an AMD Versal AI Edge Series Gen 2 board (relay sourced, and caveated: the item rested on relay accounts, allday_stocks with a Thai language corroboration, and neither vendor's account posted it; Credo's own October 13 release confirms the demonstration and the Versal board, and frames AMD's role as platform partner).

The morning's broader coverage (43 posts) carried the rest of the morning: the Applied Materials investor breakfast slide cluster from BenBajarin and BrendanBurkeX (an investor day event adjacent to the summit, covered in Section 2 and Section 9 with that label on it); the Samsung memory strategy and CXL memory expansion cluster, including 2 posts from October 12 whose coverage had lagged and was completed this morning; corroboration of the Celestica DS6005 CPO switch, including SONiC support and a Dell'Oro quote; AMD items (the AMD Newsroom keynote recap, the AMD and nVent Helios cooling collaboration, the AMD AI NIC promo with a substantive commenter observation about the Vulcano 800); the Semtech and Tower SiGe capacity expansion; the Texas Instruments 3 chip launch as reported by trade press; the optical test thread continuation naming KYEC, Sigurd, and ASE as CPO burn in and final test houses; and the Schulz Research ASML and DUV explainer.

On the Section 10 follow through, the scoreboard as of midday is: 2 items resolved outright (Helion availability, KIOXIA CM9 specifications), 1 item settled for the systems named with a session still to come (which Vera Rubin systems use CPO), 4 items advanced (Intel D270 specifications, Vicor 337-TA-1526, Credo SRMO and ALC with 2 corrections that must be carried forward, optical test capacity on names but not on capacity), 1 item largely resolved by the transcripts with 2 sub items still unreported (the Day 1 no report sessions), 4 items still open (Intel shortage and pricing, the rack forecast dispute and ODM checks, Helios volumes on numbers, and the Google 800 VDC timeline inside item 9), and the balance scheduled later today or Wednesday (Tuesday sessions, DMTF workshop, Arista, the memory wall panel). Section 10 works through all 15 items one by one.

The 2 loudest silences of the day so far are the 2 morning keynotes. The Microsoft keynote at 9:15 AM PT and the Google keynote by Partha Ranganathan at 11:10 AM PT both happened before midday, and as of midday there is no coverage of either one anywhere this report can reach: nothing in the X coverage (no post this morning mentions a Microsoft keynote or a Google keynote), nothing in trade press found by web research, no Google blog post, and no ServeTheHome, Data Center Dynamics, or HPCwire keynote report dated October 13. What today did produce on Microsoft is indirect but useful: the Maia 300 primary source that Day 1 lacked (a Scott Guthrie post on the Official Microsoft Blog dated October 12) is now located and the full specification set is in trade coverage, and Arista posted a collaboration announcement with Microsoft on a scale up solution for Maia accelerators (AristaNetworks). On Google, today produced nothing at all on the 800 VDC timeline question; the nearest sourced statement remains a pre summit trade piece describing Google at 54 V DC in racks today with a gradual move toward 800 V DC expected to take a couple of years, not attributed to the keynote.

Two October 13 primary releases were found by web research that did not appear in the X coverage at all, and both matter: Lattice Semiconductor and AMI formally launched SCMP, the Secure Control and Management Plane, as a new OCP workstream during a joint keynote this morning (Business Wire, October 13), which is the Tuesday keynote the Day 1 transcripts pointed at (the CEOs of Lattice and AMI, per Session 11 of the transcript corpus); and Astera Labs announced Aries 7, described as the industry's first PCIe 7 signal conditioning portfolio across copper and optical (October 13). SolarEdge's October 13 release on its MVAC to 800 VDC technology in the NVIDIA MGX ecosystem showcase also adds primary detail behind a headline the coverage carried in early morning coverage.

The Applied Materials material deserves a flag at the top because it is the largest single cluster in today's X record and it is not an OCP session. Applied Materials held its investor breakfast this morning (Applied's investor day is October 13, a separate event), and 2 analysts, BenBajarin and BrendanBurkeX, posted slide photographs through the morning: an agentic AI factory pod consumes 2x to 4x more wafers than a generative AI factory pod (about 600 wafers per pod for the Gen AI pod on a GB200 SuperPOD basis, about 1,400 for Agentic Config A on Rubin content, about 2,200 for Config B on Rubin Ultra HBM content), DRAM's share of the pod rises from 46% to 54% to 67% across those configurations, Applied's CY25 to CY30 targets include over 2 points of WFE share gain, 20% service revenue growth per tool, 5 points of gross margin, and 10 points of operating margin, hybrid bonding covers about 80% of the process flow in Applied's portfolio, HBM packaging SAM expands from $400M to $500M per 100K WSPM on microbump and TSV to $800M to $1B on hybrid bonding and TSV, and a late morning thread from the investor Q and A has system architects determining that some inference workloads need less DRAM than training (the HBM despec thread, Section 5). The cluster was reported this morning as analyst coverage, and SEMICON West coverage highlighted some of the same slides today. This report covers the cluster once, in Section 2 and in the thematic sections where the slides bear on summit topics, labeled as investor day material throughout.

2. THE DAY'S MAJOR DEVELOPMENTS IN DEPTH

MARVELL ALASKA E 3.2T RETIMER AND ALASKA A 1.6T AEC DSP LAUNCH (OFFICIAL POST; SPECIFICATIONS FROM THE OCTOBER 13 PRIMARY RELEASE)

The first headline of the day, posted this morning: MarvellTech, the company account, announcing a new Alaska retimer and AEC DSP launch for AI infrastructure as scale up moves to 224G per lane at 102.4T switch bandwidth. The X record's media analysis of the post's graphic is explicit about what the post itself does and does not contain: the graphic reads "EXPANDING PORTFOLIO. New Retimer and AEC DSP for AI Infrastructure" over a chip image branded MARVELL Alaska, with no specs on the graphic; the 224G per lane and 102.4T context is in the post text. No pricing or lane counts are in the post.

The specifications come from Marvell's primary release, and the distinction matters for sourcing: Marvell via Business Wire, October 13, 2026, "Marvell Bolsters Connectivity Portfolio with New 3.2T Protocol-aware Retimer and Second-generation 1.6T AEC DSP." Per the release: an Alaska E 3.2T protocol aware retimer and a second generation Alaska A 1.6T AEC DSP, both sampling to customers and shown at the summit; 8 lanes of 224G PAM4; gearbox modes from 1.6T down to 50G; support for Ethernet, UALink, and ESUN; 45 dB plus insertion loss compensation. The AEC DSP is listed at 12.8 W in a 12 mm by 14 mm package, with an 8 W saving claim versus 5 nm designs. A duplicate recap post by RedCandleRx (the same headline posted twice 32 seconds apart) names the products as "a new 3.2T retimer and a second-generation 1.6T cable chip," which matches the release naming; the coverage recorded it as a duplicate of the headline, and the product naming is press release detail for the same announcement. One thread continuation is worth recording because it is the kind of question the retimer market turns on: GP_Studios1 asked on the Alaska thread whether qualification data will report retimer power and latency at the intended cable length alongside error rates. A question, no new facts, no answer in the X record.

Context from Marvell's own October 8 summit preview (Business Wire, October 8): the booth demonstration list included Teralynx T100 102.4T switching, Structera CXL, Ara DSP 1.6T optics, 400G per lane PAM4, COLORZ 800G, 1.6T AECs, and a Bravera PCIe 6.0 SSD controller. The Alaska launch is the October 13 product news; the 400G item below is a demonstration, and the distinction is Marvell's own.

MARVELL 2NM 400G PER LANE PAM4 LIVE DEMONSTRATION (OFFICIAL POST, BOOTH PHOTOGRAPH)

Posted late this morning: MarvellTech, demonstrating what the post calls the industry's first 2nm 400G per lane PAM4 solution at the summit, Booth B31, a technology that enables the transition to 3.2T data center connectivity. The post's only link is its photo, and the photo was viewed and analyzed: a booth screen headed "Next-Generation 400G AI Connectivity" over a Keysight Eye and Mask analyzer showing live PAM4 eye diagrams (Channel 1A and F8 TDECQ), with a results panel reading RLM (802.3 CL_94) 0.944, TDECQ 0.50 dB, Outer ER 3.976 dB, Outer OMA 775.0 uW, Average Power -0.33 dBm, and a frame trigger of 226.67000 GBd with 2047 UI, consistent with 400G per lane PAM4 signaling. The X record analysis states plainly: the photo confirms a live 400G per lane demonstration; no product name or launch date is in the image.

Web research confirms the framing: there is no standalone October 13 Marvell product release for a 400G PAM4 DSP. The 400G per lane PAM4 item appears in Marvell's October 8 preview as a booth demonstration. So the correct Day 2 statement is that Marvell publicly demonstrated 2nm 400G per lane PAM4 silicon running live at its booth with published eye diagram metrics, which is a technology demonstration milestone on the road to 3.2T (8 lanes at 400G), not a product launch. The post is a headline item: an official MarvellTech demonstration post from the summit floor.

WIWYNN, AYAR LABS, AND GUC FIRST LIVE CPO DEMONSTRATION (CORROBORATED BY THE OCTOBER 13 PRIMARY RELEASE)

Posted late this morning: carrioresearch. Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and Global Unichip (GUC) are running their first live co-packaged optics demonstration at the summit: a Wiwynn compute system carrying a GUC ASIC with Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines packaged inside it, lit by an Ayar SuperNova external light source (ELSFP based), streaming the engines' real time health telemetry and proving the optical link is up inside the system; a detachable fiber array unit and in chassis fiber routing for servicing and manufacturing. Ayar CEO Mark Wade, in the quote carried in the post and in the release: "The bar is no longer whether it works; it's whether it can be deployed and managed at scale." The fuller quote, from the image analysis of the release text: "AI is driving the industry toward an optically-connected future, and the bar is no longer whether it works; it is whether it can be deployed and managed at scale," and the demonstration "is about proving integration and operability in a real platform and giving data center teams the data they will need to adopt CPO with confidence, making the next generation of AI infrastructure deployable at hyperscale." Ayar counts NVIDIA and AMD among its strategic investors; Sivers is the SuperNova light source partner.

The primary source corroborates the post. Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and GUC via PR Newswire, October 13, 2026: the 3 companies are presenting a live demonstration for the first time, a Wiwynn compute system integrating a GUC ASIC multi chip package with Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines and a SuperNova light source, with real time health telemetry polled continuously from the engines within the packages, proving the optical link is up inside the system, and with signal quality metrics held steady while the tuning subsystem tracks thermal and wavelength drift. The companies frame the step as advancing from the earlier rack level architecture collaboration to platform integration and functional validation. The X record photo shows the booth rack under "Create AI Beyond Limits" signage with a CPO Telemetry Dashboard screen and a Wiwynn CPO Compute Tray placard, and a Wiwynn CEO William Lin quote beginning at the bottom of the release screenshot (cropped in the image; the text is not in the X record). A partial quote from Sean Tai, President of GUC, is also visible in a follow up crop: integrating optical I/O directly into chip design and proving functionality through live system level demonstration is a significant achievement in the collaboration (rest cropped). No bandwidth figure, customer, or ship date is given in the release material returned. That absence is itself the data point: the demonstration's claim is operability (telemetry, drift tracking, serviceable fiber), not a bandwidth record.

A follow up carrioresearch post (also posted this morning) adds the operational detail: the demo puts telemetry, transmitter heater activity, and eye metrics on screen, the numbers an operations team wants. Its photo is a crop from the same release; no new specs or numbers.

Why this item leads the optics day: Day 1's CPO record was roadmaps, claims, and a standardization launch (Credo SRMO), plus Micas field data from a Monday session reported in this morning's coverage (hundreds of CPO switches at a hyperscaler about 18 months ago). The Wiwynn, Ayar, and GUC demonstration is the first Day 2 item that is a live, running, multi vendor CPO system on the show floor with the management layer working, which is exactly the deployability question the Day 1 open ecosystem sessions (transcript Sessions 36 and 40) said would decide the 2027 inflection. It is not a Vera Rubin system; it is CPO evidence, not a platform ship claim.

OCP AND IDC MARKET IMPACT STUDY: 2029 FORECAST RAISED 2.7X TO $800B (OFFICIAL POST, VERIFIED AGAINST THE FOUNDATION RELEASE)

Posted this morning: OpenComputePrj, the Foundation account, announcing at the summit today the latest IDC Market Impact Study. The post's infographic was viewed and analyzed, and the numbers are: IDC raises the 2029 forecast for OCP recognized infrastructure spending by 2.7x to $800B (2.7x higher than last year's forecast for the same year); projected annual spending on OCP recognized IT equipment reaches $892B in 2030; 51% by 2030 of spending across the infrastructure categories measured will go to OCP recognized infrastructure; $628B in AI related spending by 2030 on OCP recognized infrastructure, about 70% of the forecast total. The study was commissioned by the Open Compute Project Foundation.

The Foundation's own release (Open Compute Project Foundation, October 13, 2026, also via PR Newswire) adds the path and the base: last year's forecast for 2029 was $295B; the path given is about $154B in 2025 to $892B in 2030, about 42% CAGR, with servers the largest category. Two caveats belong on this item wherever it is used. First, it is an OCP commissioned outlook, not booked revenue, orders, or shipments; it measures spending on equipment that conforms to OCP recognized specifications across covered categories. Second, a discrepancy to flag, not merge: the Day 1 welcome session speaker, as captured in the transcript corpus (Session 18), said 890 billion dollars for 2030, while the Foundation post and release say $892B. The transcript deep dive's read, which this report adopts, is that one side or the other is rounding; the sourced figure is $892B, and the 890 figure is recorded as spoken.

CREDO OMNICONNECT WEAVER ON AMD VERSAL (RELAY SOURCED; THE OCTOBER 13 CREDO RELEASE CONFIRMS THE DEMONSTRATION)

First reported this morning: "Credo collaborates with AMD to expand AI accelerator memory capacity and bandwidth using OmniConnect Weaver technology; working memory expansion platform demonstrated on AMD Versal AI Edge Gen 2 at OCP Global Summit 2026, terabyte-class per headline." The note in the X record states the sourcing plainly: relayed by allday_stocks, corroborated by a Thai language post, no prior posts on X about OmniConnect, genuinely new. Neither Credo's nor AMD's account posted the item, and the item carried that caveat when it was reported.

Credo's primary release, found by web research, confirms the core and narrows the framing. Credo via Business Wire, October 13, 2026, "Credo Breaks the Memory Wall Using AMD Programmable Logic-Based AI Accelerators": Credo is demonstrating its OmniConnect Weaver memory fanout gearbox running on an AMD Versal AI Edge Series Gen 2 adaptive SoC evaluation board at the summit, Booth B2. The claim is terabyte class LPDDR capacity and high bandwidth to a programmable logic device over VSR links on standard organic packaging, with no silicon interposer, and application software running unmodified. AMD's role in the release is the Versal platform partner; the release does not describe an Instinct collaboration. So the Day 2 position is: the demonstration is real and primary confirmed; the "Credo collaborating with AMD" headline framing came from relay accounts and overstates what the release says, which is a Credo memory fanout product demonstrated on AMD programmable logic hardware. A duplicate re share of the same demo was not counted twice. Section 10, item 7, tracks what this does and does not do for the Credo SRMO and ALC questions: nothing. Weaver is a different product, and the SRMO identity questions remain exactly where the transcripts left them.

One small change to the actor update makes RL work for flow policies on real robots, VLAs, and even image models. Here's QF3 from UC Berkeley and Amazon FAR, explained in 4 minutes!!!

A lot of robots today run on flow policies. A flow policy turns random noise into an action by following a learned velocity field, one small step at a time. Think of it as diffusion for actions. You normally train one by imitation, on a dataset of demonstrations.

Reinforcement learning is harder, because there's no dataset. The robot only has its own attempts in a replay buffer. You train a critic, Q, to score actions. The most direct way to improve the policy is then to follow the critic's gradient: predict where the flow lands in one step, and push it uphill on Q.

The catch is that if that prediction lands far from anything in the buffer, the critic is guessing. When it overestimates, the policy chases a fake peak and training falls apart which is not at all what we want!

QF3's fix is to clip the policy's velocity so its prediction stays close to the replay action, where the critic can be trusted. Past the clip, the gradient is simply masked out. It's one actor update, with a standard critic and no extra networks.

The results are pretty promising 
• Fine-tuning a pretrained bimanual VLA (ABC-VLA) with only LoRA adapters on its flow action head, VLM frozen. In the side-by-side episodes, the QF3 policy finishes bottles-in-bin 1.8× faster and plates-in-dish-rack 2.1× faster than the base policy. 
• Full fine-tuning on the robomimic Square, Tool Hang and Transport tasks. 
• Humanoids trained from scratch: they dropped QF3 into FastTD3 unchanged and deployed on real hardware for velocity tracking and motion tracking. Yes, it dances. On motion tracking it reached the same performance about 10× faster in wall-clock time than FPO++, on a single GPU. 
• The same update fine-tunes Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Each prompt is a one-step episode, and the PickScore reward model plays the critic.

I like this because it's the most direct way to use a critic, made safe with a one-line idea: only trust the gradient where the critic has seen data. Teleoperated demonstrations are slow and expensive, and a policy that RL can make faster and better after imitation is a big deal.

Code is "coming soon." Project page and paper are in the reply.

What would you fine-tune with this first: a manipulation policy, a humanoid, or an image model?

Research|META: Muse Wonder Returns Meta to the Frontier as Compute Tightens
Personal agents expand Meta’s opportunity as training and inference demand put more pressure on compute capacity

On October 12, Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, the models previously referred to in reports as Watermelon. These are Meta’s first frontier models since Llama 4, arriving 14 months after Alexandr Wang reorganized the company’s AI teams in August 2025. Both were trained on Meta’s Prometheus cluster in Ohio, support text, image, audio, and video inputs, and have a 1M-token context window. Neither model’s weights are publicly available.

Wonder is available through the Meta Model API and Muse Code at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Wonder Full is available only to Muse Code subscribers on the $50 and $200 monthly plans, with no API access. Our channel checks indicate that Wonder has roughly 3T total parameters, making it smaller than both Astra and Fable.

We believe Meta is back among the leading frontier AI labs, and we expect it to stay there. In our view, a year ago that group consisted mainly of OpenAI and Anthropic. Google rejoined this year, followed by Meta, and a four-way contest is taking shape. The hiring spree in the summer of 2025 is paying off: backed by substantial investment in compute, the new team brought Meta back to the frontier in just over a year.

Compute remains the biggest bottleneck. According to media reports, in July Meta was preparing to rent out surplus GPUs and was in talks with Anthropic; by October, its own needs had forced it to shelve the plan. Anthropic, meanwhile, secured new capacity from other suppliers and raised usage limits when it launched Opus 5.5. We expect the shortage to ease only once Vera Rubin and TPU 8t ship in volume in 2027. We also expect Meta’s 2027 capex to rise again. On open-weight models, we maintain our September view that the gap between the leading open-weight models and the top closed models will widen again to 6 to 12 months.

Every AI agent needs somewhere to work. But what happens when a startup needs to give every customer their own AI agent?

The infrastructure quickly becomes another problem to solve. @AryShriv and @mariagorskikh saw this challenge while hosting hundreds of agents during their research at MIT.

Getting environments running was only part of the work. Maintaining them and debugging individual agents took time too. So they started building @maritime_sh.

Maritime (YC F26) is a managed cloud platform that gives every AI agent its own isolated, persistent virtual machine. Each agent gets a computer where it can run code, install software, use a browser, and retain files and logins between tasks.

Maritime (YC F26) manages the infrastructure around those environments, including deployment, scaling, and automatic sleep and wake. The goal is simple: help startups give every customer their own AI agent without having to manage the underlying cloud infrastructure themselves.

Hosting starts at $1 per agent per month, and developers can try three agents for free. The bigger opportunity isn't just building smarter AI agents. Its making the infrastructure behind them practical to deploy and scale.

For founders building AI products, the lesson is worth considering: the product is only part of the challenge. The infrastructure behind every customer experience matters too.

Congratulations to @mariagorskikh and @AryShriv on building @maritime_sh.

@loopsai_global has raised a $3.5M seed. @speedrun, @nttcom Ventures, Connecticut Innovations, @alumniventures  and Monday Capital all put in. It follows a $400K round in September 2025 led by Monday Capital and Mantra.

Loops is one AI system behind a retailer's whole shop: search, the shopping assistant, product listings and virtual try-on. Most retailers buy those four separately and wire them together. Loops runs them off a single catalogue, so each one improves the next. Better listings make search better, and what shoppers ask shows which listings are thin. More than 70 customers and pilots so far, and 64% of pilots become paying customers.

Ari Nazir, CEO and co-founder, is an a16z speedrun scout and has been an entrepreneur since school. He built the first version of Loops over a weekend in Bali.

İlker Selim Zorluoğlu, president and co-founder, was chief strategy officer at GoArt for three years, where the team went from 10 to 100 people, and CMO at Roam Network, taking its audience from 5,000 to over 100,000 in six months.

Yusuf Bahadır, CTO and co-founder, spent six years at RoofStacks architecting products across fintech, XR, gaming and enterprise software, and studied scientific computation and parallel programming at Istanbul Technical University.
